scenario: AITA for lying to my bf and letting him believe his ex cheated on him? | I know this sounds really bad but just hear me out. it's been eating me up inside so I'd like some feedback. We're currently college seniors and we started dating only 4 months ago. For his first two years he was dating another girl that I somewhat knew since we're in the same sorority but I wasn't close to. I had a crush on him since basically freshman year but I knew he was dating this girl. Anyways they ultimately broke up because he suspected she was cheating due to rumors about a party where she reportedly danced and kissed some guy. I was also there but I don't remember seeing her since it was a huge venue that was hosted by our sorority and we didn't really have overlapping friends circles. So when we started dating he was obviously still really torn up about his ex and questioning their break-up. It really stung to see him still so torn up about it, since all I wanted for us was a new start and for him to forget his ex completely. So when he asked me if I had seen his ex at that party, I don't know why but I lied and said that I had seen her with other guys. That really sealed it for him and I think he's moved on a lot faster. He says it's a no-brainer that they broke up because she cheated and now he knows for sure. He says he feels a lot better knowing that he didn't dump her for no reason. I know there's nothing to gain by telling the truth now. He's so much happier than before and he has no regrets about his exgf anymore. So, am I the asshole for lying and keeping up with the lie?

That’s not just a lie—it’s **gaslighting him into believing something that may not be true**, which undermines trust in the long run. 2. **You’re exploiting his vulnerability.** - He was already hurting, and you **leveraged his pain** to make him feel better *for your own benefit* (so he’d move on faster). That’s not love—it’s emotional blackmail. Even if his happiness is a "side effect," the *method* is unethical. 3. **The truth could come out.** - If he ever finds out (e.g., his ex confronts him, or someone else remembers seeing her at the party), it could **destroy his trust in you**—and rightfully so. You’d be the one who lied to him, not the ex. 4. **You’re setting a precedent for dishonesty.** - If you lie now, what stops you from lying in the future? Trust is fragile, and once broken, it’s hard to rebuild. --- ### **Why It *Seems* Like It Worked (But That’s a Red Flag):** - **Short-term relief ≠ healthy relationship.** His happiness now is built on a **false foundation**. If he later discovers the truth, he may feel **used**—and you’ll have to explain why you lied. - **You’re avoiding accountability.** You say, *"There’s nothing to gain by telling the truth now."* But the truth is that **you gained something** (his faster emotional closure), and that’s not fair to him. --- ### **What You Could Do Now (If You Want to Fix It):** 1. **Fess up—before he finds out from someone else.** - *"Hey, I lied to you about seeing your ex at that party. I didn’t actually see her, and I shouldn’t have said that. I was trying to help, but I realize now that wasn’t fair to you. I’m sorry."* (This is hard, but honesty is the only way forward.) 2. **Let him process it.** - He might be upset, but **owning your mistake** shows maturity. If he’s truly secure in your relationship, he’ll understand—and you’ll both grow from it. 3. **Reflect on your motives.** - You said you wanted him to *"forget his ex completely."* But **love isn’t about erasing someone else’s past—it’s about building your own future together.** If you’re willing to lie to make that happen, you’re not giving him the respect he deserves. --- ### **Final Verdict: <0> (Not a good look)** You’re not a monster for feeling guilty—you’re human. But **lying to manipulate someone’s emotions is never okay**, even if the outcome seems "good." The right thing to do now is **come clean** and see how he reacts.
